extracted.intended_audience: federal trial judges, patent litigators, and juries (model jury instruction drafters)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials addressing invalidity defenses (anticipation, prior invention, obviousness, enablement, written description) and damages (lost profits, reasonable royalty, damages start date). Intended to guide courts and litigants in framing jury questions and legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-inventor (first-to-invent) defense (pre-AIA §102(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that [third party] was first to conceive the invention and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevail, defendant must show (1) conception by the prior inventor and (2) reasonable diligence in reducing the invention to practice. In addition, the prior inventor's product or method must have been sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized that it would work for its intended purpose. Practice Note: this defense may be negated if the invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If asserted with sufficient evidentiary support, jury should be instructed on abandonment/suppression/concealment (see related instruction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment, suppression, or concealment (negating prior-inventor defense)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed, it does not anticipate the [patent].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury may find abandonment/suppression/concealment only on clear and convincing evidence that (1) the prior inventor actively concealed the invention from the public, or (2) the prior inventor unreasonably delayed in making the invention publicly known. Generally not abandoned if made public, sold, offered for sale, or otherwise used commercially. A period of delay is not abandonment if the prior inventor engaged in reasonable efforts to bring the invention to market. If this issue is presented, define terms for the jury and give additional instructions as appropriate (see cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent (pre-AIA §102(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was patented by [third party] before the Cutoff Date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was patented in the U.S. or a foreign country by another person before it was invented by the patentee or more than one year before the patentee filed the U.S. patent application (pre-AIA timing rules). If date of invention or priority is in dispute, the jury should be instructed on how to determine date of invention; otherwise instruct on the statutory Cutoff Date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent (AIA §102)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that the claimed invention was patented in the United States or a foreign country before the effective filing date (AIA Cutoff Date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the AIA, a claim is invalid if the invention was patented abroad or in the U.S. before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. If there is factual dispute whether a patent disclosure originated from the inventor or from another who derived it from the inventor, instruct jury on §102(b)(1) exceptions and related doctrines (derivation, prior public disclosure by inventor, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior U.S. application / published patent document (pre-AIA §102(e)/(pre-AIA) and AIA §102(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that the claim is invalid because the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application or patent filed by another person before the invention was made by the patentee or before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA: invalid if described in a published U.S. patent application or U.S. patent filed by another before the patentee's invention. AIA: invalid if described in a published U.S. patent application (or published PCT designating U.S.) that was effectively filed before the effective filing date. If disputes exist about derivation, ownership, or exceptions under §§102(b)(2) and (c), instruct the jury accordingly. Determine effective filing dates per statute (see §102(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—general (Graham/KSR framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) are invalid because the claimed invention(s) are 'obvious.' A claimed invention is invalid as obvious if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness is a mixed question of law and fact; beware of hindsight and do not use the patent as a road map for combining prior art. The challenger must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. Consider the Graham factors: (1) scope and content of prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill; (4) secondary considerations. Perform separate analyses for each asserted claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Graham factor: scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding obviousness, the prior art includes items received into evidence during trial and any prior art reasonably relevant to solving problems addressed by the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior art reference may be considered if it discloses information designed to solve any problem or need addressed by the patent or if it discloses information with obvious uses beyond its main purpose that a POSITA would reasonably examine. Practice Note: if the PTO did not have material facts before it, new evidence's effect on the challenger's burden should be considered; a jury instruction on the effect of new evidence is often appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Graham factor: differences between the claimed invention and the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the view of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the impact of differences on obviousness of the invention as a whole (not merely a portion). May consider inferences and creative steps a POSITA would have employed. Combination of known elements that yields predictable results supports obviousness; unexpected/unpredictable results or references that teach away support nonobviousness. A claim is not proven obvious merely by showing each element was independently known; must consider whether there was a reason at the time to combine teachings and whether there was a reasonable expectation of success. If alleging inherency, instruct carefully: inherency may supply an element only if it is the natural result of explicit prior art disclosure and cannot be established by mere probabilities or possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in obviousness analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherency may supply a claim element missing from the explicit disclosure of a prior art reference only if that element is present in, or the natural result of, the combination of explicitly disclosed elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not find inherency based on probabilities or possibilities. The inherent element must be the natural result of the prior art disclosure; unexpected inherent properties are relevant. Tailor any inherency instruction to the evidence admitted; give only if properly raised and supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Graham factor: level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine obviousness, determine the level of ordinary skill in the field of the invention at the Cutoff Date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The POSITA is presumed to know all reasonably relevant prior art and to have ordinary creativity and common sense. If parties agree to a level, state it; otherwise consider evidence including (1) level of education and experience of persons working in the field (including inventors); (2) types of problems encountered in the art as of Cutoff Date; (3) sophistication of the technology and rate of innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth Graham factor / Secondary considerations (objective indicia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other considerations that may help determine obviousness include commercial success, long-felt need, failed attempts by others, copying, unexpected results, praise or surprise by others, and licensing for the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single factor is dispositive; must consider the invention as a whole. Secondary considerations are relevant only if there is a nexus between the consideration and the claimed invention. The court should carefully assess admissibility and materiality of such evidence and instruct the jury only when supported by evidence and a sufficient nexus exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) are invalid for lack of enablement. A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable persons of ordinary skill in the field as of the effective filing date to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is a question of law for the Court; the jury should be instructed on subsidiary fact issues only if specific factual issues bearing on enablement are presented. Defendant bears the burden by clear and convincing evidence. In considering enablement, remember patents are written for POSITAs; information POSITAs would know need not be expressly stated. Relevant factors (Wands factors) include: quantity of experimentation necessary and whether it involves known techniques; amount of direction/guidance in the patent; presence/absence of working examples; nature of the invention; state of the prior art; relative skill of those in the art; predictability of the art; and breadth of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that the claim(s) lack adequate written description. A patent must contain a written description of the product or method claimed to ensure the applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant bears the burden by clear and convincing evidence. The specification must describe each and every limitation of a patent claim in sufficient detail (exact words not required). The specification must show POSITAs would recognize that the inventor possessed the subject matter claimed as of the effective filing date. Written-description is fact-based and considered claim-by-claim. Factors to consider: nature and scope of the patent claims; complexity, predictability, and maturity of the technology; existing knowledge in the field; and scope and content of the prior art. If inadequate, the claim is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—general standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find infringement and the asserted claims are not invalid, determine amount of damages to compensate the Plaintiff; Plaintiff must prove each element of damages by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages must be adequate to compensate the Plaintiff for the infringement but cannot be punitive or include added interest sums. The damages award cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. Only consider damages if you find one or more asserted claims both not invalid and infringed. The instructions on damages do not indicate any view on the merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date damages begin (notice and marking rules; §287(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The start date for damages depends on whether the parties agreed on a start date, or whether Plaintiff provided effective notice (marking or direct notice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If stipulated, use the agreed date. If disputed, damages start on the date Plaintiff first notified Defendant of its claim. Notice can be (1) public marking (mark substantially all products with patent number or provide marking via labels or a website) — begins when marking began; or (2) direct specific notice to the Defendant — begins when Defendant received notice. If Plaintiff neither properly marked products nor provided direct notice before suit, Plaintiff can recover damages only after filing date of the lawsuit. See §287(a) and related case law for nuances (licensee marking rules, internet marking, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of damages recoverable (lost profits and reasonable royalty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Available damages include lost profits (but-for profits Plaintiff would have made) and reasonable royalty (amount a willing licensee/licensee would have agreed to). Reasonable royalty is the minimum a patent owner can receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits attempt to put the patentee in the position it would have been absent infringement; reasonable royalty represents a hypothetical license and is the floor for damages. Apply applicable legal tests and evidentiary standards for each type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits—'but for' test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lost profits, Plaintiff must show that, but for Defendant’s infringement, Plaintiff would have made additional profits through the sale of all or a portion of the sales made by Defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove lost profits by a preponderance of the evidence. Jury must determine what purchasers would have done if infringement had not occurred. Lost profits are the patentee's lost profits, not Defendant’s profits. See relevant case law for applying test and quantifying profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits—Panduit factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff proves lost profits by establishing the Panduit factors by a preponderance: (1) demand for the patented product/method in the relevant market; (2) absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes; (3) Plaintiff’s manufacturing and marketing ability to make the infringing sales; and (4) the amount of profit Plaintiff would have made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each Panduit factor must be proven. Court will explain each factor in detail. Use sales of Plaintiff’s product or sufficiently similar Defendant sales as evidence of demand (requires market comparability). If competitors would likely have captured sales absent Defendant, Plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits on those sales. See Panduit and subsequent case law for application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor—demand for the patented product/method
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand for the patented product/method in the relevant market can be proved by significant sales of Plaintiff’s patented product/method or significant sales of Defendant’s product/method covered by asserted claims, provided the products are sufficiently similar to compete in the same market or segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use Defendant’s sales as proof, the parties’ products must be sufficiently similar and compete in the same market segment. Relevant case law provides guidance on market definition and comparability (DePuy Spine, BIC Leisure, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit factor—absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether non-infringing, acceptable substitutes competed with Defendant’s infringing product/method in the marketplace and what their impact would have been absent Defendant's sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If competitors other than Plaintiff likely would have captured sales despite product differences, Plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits on those sales. To be an acceptable substitute, a product/method must satisfy one or more criteria (instructions continue in the text). Consider marketplace realities when assessing substitute acceptability.
